edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SPORT + SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY
edition.deck: Violence and political pressure across France and Ukraine, a deadly fire at a Canadian base, and fresh developments in British and Danish public life.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises overnight developments and substantial fresh reporting. Continuing stories from the previous edition are included only where this gather adds a significant development or a new dimension.

content.headline: Macron urges calm after France’s riots as questions mount over policing
content.shortHeadline: Macron urges calm as questions mount over France’s riots
content.standfirst: After a weekend of protests and widespread looting, France’s president has promised transparency about the police response. Political leaders are already disputing who was responsible for the violence and what should follow.

image.caption: The 19th-century town hall in Limoges was gutted by fire during the unrest.

sources.originalTitle: Macron calls for 'calm and order' after riots across France
Macron criticises ‘unbridled violence’ after days of unrest and 2,400 arrests across France
Macron calls for calm after ‘extremely violent’ protests gripped France
Macron forsøgte at række hånden ud til demonstranter i tale, siger korrespondent

segments.body: Some 550,000 people joined largely peaceful demonstrations in France over the cost of living, fuel prices and public services, according to the interior minister. Separate groups clashed with police, set fires and looted shops; more than 2,400 people were arrested, and police reported nearly 1,000 officers and gendarmes injured.

segments.title: A disputed response
segments.body: President Emmanuel Macron drew a distinction between peaceful demonstrators and those who looted or attacked buildings, and promised “full transparency” over the police response. Politicians and local officials have questioned the authorities’ handling of events; left-wing figures have also accused police of provoking clashes.

DR correspondent Stéphanie Surrugue said Macron’s address also acknowledged protesters’ concerns about living costs and fuel prices. She warned that the political fallout may continue as presidential hopefuls confront the economic problems and public anger they could inherit.

perspectives.body: DR’s correspondent in Paris interpreted Macron’s speech as both a condemnation of violence and an attempt to reach out to people protesting about living costs and rising diesel prices.

content.headline: Four soldiers dead and 39 injured in fire at Canadian military base
content.shortHeadline: Four soldiers dead after fire at Canadian military base
content.standfirst: A fire broke out during training at CFB Wainwright in Alberta and is now contained. The cause remains under investigation; officials say the incident does not appear to involve outside interference.

sources.originalTitle: Major fire at Canada military base leaves four dead, dozens injured
Fire døde og 39 sårede i gårsdagens brand på canadisk militærbase

segments.body: Four Canadian military personnel died and 39 people were injured in a fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta. At least 19 of those injured were in critical condition, provincial officials said. The fire, which broke out on Saturday, is contained, but crews remain at the scene.

segments.title: How the fire spread
segments.body: A grass fire in the training area spread towards a range used for live-fire exercises. A senior military officer said unusually strong winds caused it to change direction and spread rapidly. The cause of the grass fire remains under investigation.

Emergency teams treated and transferred patients to hospitals across Alberta. The cause of the fire has not been established. The Canadian Armed Forces said there were no current indications of terrorist activity; a senior officer said investigators did not believe it was linked to outside interference or oil and gas infrastructure.

content.headline: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as US-Ukraine tensions deepen
content.shortHeadline: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as US tensions deepen
content.standfirst: Attacks hit sites and cities on both sides as a proposed energy truce falters. Kyiv says US intelligence-sharing has resumed, but its claims about restrictions on Starlink are disputed by the Trump administration.

image.caption: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

sources.originalTitle: Ukraine war briefing: Trump accuses Zelenskyy of not wanting to end war as feud rumbles on
Zelenskyy thanks Trump for resumed intelligence sharing after US Starlink ‘message’
Zelenskyj takker USA for igen at dele efterretninger med Ukraine

segments.body: Ukrainian strikes set fires at an oil terminal and depot in the St Petersburg region, while Russian attacks hit Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. Local officials reported deaths and injuries on both sides. The exchanges came after a short-lived proposed energy ceasefire failed to stop attacks.

segments.title: A dispute with Washington
segments.body: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy thanked the US for restoring intelligence-sharing about Russian missile attacks, after a period when it was blocked. He also said US officials had deliberately limited Ukraine’s Starlink access. US officials have denied that accusation, and responsibility for the restrictions remains disputed.

segments.title: Strikes near NATO territory
segments.body: Lithuania briefly warned residents to shelter after an unidentified object entered its airspace. Ukraine said it regretted the incident and suggested Russian electronic warfare may have diverted a drone. Lithuanian authorities said the object had crossed from Poland; its full circumstances remain unclear.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s briefing also reports a suspected arson attempt at a Lithuanian company hosting Starlink equipment. Lithuania’s prime minister blamed Russia, but the report says authorities had not publicly identified the company’s location.

content.headline: Guardian reports witnessing settlers attack European delegation in West Bank
content.shortHeadline: Guardian says it witnessed settlers attack European visitors
content.standfirst: The Guardian says its reporters saw masked men attack a European delegation in Taybeh, including a French mayor. Israel’s prime minister’s office has questioned whether the available images establish the sequence of events or responsibility.

sources.originalTitle: Guardian reporter filmed masked militants seconds before West Bank attack on French mayor

segments.body: The Guardian says its journalists witnessed masked men approach and attack a group of European diplomats, French clerics and visitors in the Palestinian town of Taybeh. The delegation had been leaving after a visit to olive groves. The report says video captured the moments before a French mayor was assaulted and footage showed an attack on the group’s vehicle as it drove away.

segments.title: Disputed account
segments.body: Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said images alone did not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility, and raised concerns about what it called a campaign to smear Israel. The Guardian challenges that account, saying its reporters were present and that video and other material support the eyewitness description.

content.headline: China’s growth picks up as AI exports offset weak domestic spending
content.shortHeadline: China’s growth picks up, but weak domestic demand persists
content.standfirst: China’s economy grew 4.5% in the third quarter, helped by technology exports, but weak consumer spending and a deep property slump continue to weigh on the outlook.

sources.originalTitle: China's growth accelerates as AI export boom outweighs domestic weakness

segments.body: China’s economy grew 4.5% in the three months to the end of September, up from 4.3% in the previous quarter but below the 5% growth recorded at the start of the year, official figures show. The result is at the lower end of Beijing’s annual target.

segments.title: Exports and domestic weakness
segments.body: Demand for chips and other components used in AI data centres has helped lift exports, while household spending and investment remain weak. Property investment fell by more than 20% in the first nine months of the year compared with the same period in 2025, and analysts say there is little sign the property slump is ending.

China’s large trade surplus is drawing concern from the US and European Union, whose manufacturers face competition from Chinese goods. Analysts also warn that heavy spending on AI infrastructure could prove difficult to justify if expected returns do not materialise.

content.headline: Synthetic drugs are reshaping the US overdose crisis, report finds
content.shortHeadline: Synthetic drugs are reshaping the US overdose crisis
content.standfirst: Fentanyl is increasingly mixed with other synthetic drugs, creating new overdose risks that naloxone may not reverse. Recovery workers and officials say the changing supply is affecting both street users and people in jail.

image.caption: Officers search cells at Cook County jail for drug-soaked paper.

sources.originalTitle: A wave of homemade, synthetic drugs sweeps US and deepens crisis

segments.body: In Ohio and Illinois, the BBC reports that drugs sold as crack or fentanyl are increasingly mixed with synthetic substances, including sedatives that can slow breathing and are not reversed by naloxone. Drug samples and accounts from users and recovery workers illustrate how unpredictable the supply has become.

segments.title: A changing crisis
segments.body: US overdose deaths have fallen from a peak of about 110,000 in 2022 to around 70,000 last year, according to the report, but specialists warn the crisis has not ended. In Cook County jail, officials describe a separate threat: synthetic drugs soaked into paper and smuggled to prisoners, linked to fatal seizures.

A sheriff and recovery workers argue that enforcement alone will not solve the problem, and call for more treatment and support. The BBC’s reporting also describes how drug users and community groups are adapting through drug testing, naloxone distribution and recovery programmes.

content.headline: Bollywood star Tiger Shroff survives shooting in Mumbai
content.shortHeadline: Actor Tiger Shroff survives shooting in Mumbai
content.standfirst: Indian police say the actor was not hit when gunmen fired at his car as it left a football club. Two people, including his driver, were reported injured; police are investigating.

sources.originalTitle: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff survives shooting in Mumbai

segments.body: Tiger Shroff survived a shooting in Mumbai on Sunday evening and was not wounded, police said. Video published by news outlets shows gunmen firing several shots at a car as it moved past a crowd near a football club in the suburb of Juhu.

Police are investigating the attack. Local media reported that two people, including Shroff’s driver, were injured. Maharashtra’s deputy chief minister said the actor and his mother were shaken by the incident.

content.headline: Ukraine steelmaker says EU import tariffs threaten its wartime exports
content.shortHeadline: Ukraine’s steel industry seeks relief from EU import tariffs
content.standfirst: Metinvest’s chief executive says EU steel restrictions fail to account for Ukraine’s wartime circumstances. The European Commission says it considered Ukraine’s situation but acknowledges its quota is below previous levels.

sources.originalTitle: EU tariffs aimed at China hitting Ukraine, steel boss says

segments.body: Yuriy Ryzhenkov, chief executive of Ukrainian steelmaker Metinvest, says new EU import restrictions unfairly group Ukraine with countries targeted over cheap steel. He is calling for an exemption or other arrangement that would preserve Ukrainian access to the European market.

segments.title: A crucial export market
segments.body: The EU has reduced the amount of steel that can enter without tariffs and set a Ukraine-specific quota. The European Commission says the policy took Ukraine’s difficult situation into account, while acknowledging the quota is lower than in past years. Ukraine’s steel industry estimates exports to the EU could ultimately fall by 50–60%.

The industry is already under pressure from Russian attacks. Ryzhenkov says strikes have intensified and that one period in September saw no steel produced in Ukraine. He warns the coming winter could be among the hardest the industry has faced.

content.headline: One million young people are not in work or education, review author says
content.shortHeadline: Review author calls for new support for young people out of work
content.standfirst: Alan Milburn argues that employment support for young people should be funded by redirecting some welfare spending. His review says a record one million 18- to 24-year-olds are not in education, employment or training.

image.caption: Alan Milburn, author of the review into young people not in education, employment or training.

sources.originalTitle: Cut benefits to fund work support for young people, says Neet review author Alan Milburn

segments.body: A government review has identified a record one million people aged 18 to 24 who are not in education, employment or training. Alan Milburn, who is leading the review, says the problem is not simply cyclical youth unemployment: 60% of those affected have never had a job.

segments.title: Support and funding
segments.body: Milburn says ministers should shift some spending from benefits to employment support, arguing that young people need help to find and keep work. He says the system should better integrate employment, health and benefits services, and that investment is needed before any savings can be expected.

The final review has been delayed until after the budget. Milburn says poor mental health is part of the problem and argues for earlier help and more opportunities. He also says young people should be expected to take up support; his proposals have not yet been published in full.

content.headline: Police investigate Reform mayor over alleged sexualised images shown to staffer
content.shortHeadline: Reform mayor under police investigation over image allegations
content.standfirst: A female colleague says Luke Campbell showed her naked images and that she was later forced out of her job. Campbell has not commented; Reform says he firmly denies the allegations.

image.caption: Luke Campbell with Reform UK leader Nigel Farage in 2025.

sources.originalTitle: Police investigate Reform mayor for allegedly sharing ‘naked and sexualised’ images of himself

segments.body: Humberside police are investigating allegations that Luke Campbell, the Reform UK mayor of Hull and East Yorkshire, showed a senior female colleague naked and sexualised images of himself at work. The woman says she felt shocked and humiliated and that an offer of a permanent role was later withdrawn.

segments.title: Responses and process
segments.body: Campbell has not responded to requests for comment. Reform UK says he firmly denies the allegations and describes them as part of a workplace dispute. The combined authority says its standards and complaints procedures must be carried out fairly and independently.

content.headline: Labour split emerges over Andy Burnham’s plan for electoral reform
content.shortHeadline: Labour divided over Burnham’s electoral reform plans
content.standfirst: Lord Blunkett and several Labour MPs warn against replacing first-past-the-post, while supporters say the system needs an independent review. The divide raises questions about whether reform will be a priority for the party.

image.caption: Andy Burnham has called for an electoral reform commission and a manifesto commitment to change the system.

sources.originalTitle: Blunkett leads Labour backlash against Burnham’s voting reform

segments.body: Andy Burnham has proposed an electoral reform commission and a manifesto commitment to change the voting system. Lord Blunkett, a former home secretary and Labour figure, argues that proportional representation could give smaller parties disproportionate influence and weaken the link between MPs and constituencies.

segments.title: Arguments within the party
segments.body: Several Labour MPs interviewed by the i Paper oppose a shift to proportional representation, citing concerns about coalition politics, party leadership control over candidate lists and the loss of constituency representation. Some also question whether changing the system should take priority over other policy commitments.

Supporters of reform say the current system can allow a government to take office with a small share of the vote and argue that a commission should examine alternatives. MP Alex Sobel says an independent process could address concerns while retaining a constituency link. No new voting system has been chosen.

content.headline: UK steelmakers face biggest electricity-cost gap with France in three years
content.shortHeadline: UK steelmakers’ electricity-cost gap with France widens
content.standfirst: UK Steel says British steelmakers now pay almost £30 more per megawatt hour than French rivals, as high gas prices feed into electricity costs. The industry is pressing the government for further help.

image.caption: British Steel’s Scunthorpe works.

sources.originalTitle: Electricity costs put UK steelmakers in worst position in three years against EU rivals

segments.body: British steelmakers’ electricity costs are almost £30 per megawatt hour higher than those of French competitors, the largest gap in three years, according to analysis by the industry group UK Steel. The group says rising global gas prices have widened the difference.

segments.title: Pressure for more support
segments.body: The UK’s wholesale electricity price is linked to gas, while France relies more heavily on nuclear power. UK Steel argues that a price cap is needed to help steelmakers compete, estimating its proposed scheme would cost about £51m a year.

The government says it is cutting electricity bills for manufacturing businesses and electricity-intensive firms. It says the measures will reduce costs by around £1bn a year for the latter group; UK Steel says further action is needed for the sector.

content.headline: UK home sellers cut asking prices at fastest rate in 15 years
content.shortHeadline: More than 3,000 UK homes a day had asking-price cuts in September
content.standfirst: Rightmove says sellers reduced prices on more than 3,000 properties a day in September, amid a glut of homes and cautious buyers. Sales agreed were also down year on year, according to Zoopla.

sources.originalTitle: Home sellers cut asking prices on 3,000 properties a day

segments.body: Sellers cut the asking prices of more than 3,000 homes a day on average in Britain in September, the highest monthly total in 15 years, according to Rightmove data shared with the BBC. The average reduction was nearly 7%, or about £21,000 on a typical home.

segments.title: More choice for buyers
segments.body: Rightmove says homes with a price reduction typically took 119 days to find a buyer, compared with 39 days for properties listed at one price. Zoopla says the number of homes for sale rose 5% year on year in September, while agreed sales fell 9%.

Mortgage rates and tight household budgets are making buyers more selective, the property portals say. September is often a busy month for price cuts as sellers try to complete before year-end, but the data also points to a market where overpricing can leave homes on the market longer.

content.headline: Roofing fraud was the most common scam reported to Citizens Advice
content.shortHeadline: Citizens Advice warns of widespread roofing scams
content.standfirst: A Yorkshire gang convicted of defrauding homeowners took more than £1m through unnecessary or poor-quality work, while one victim’s family says the fraud accelerated his decline. Citizens Advice says roofing scams were its most common fraud complaint.

image.caption: Nicola Lamb with her father, Michael Cooper, who paid £61,000 to a roofing fraud gang.

sources.originalTitle: Cowboy builders scammed my dad of £61,000 – then his life fell apart

segments.body: A gang that pressured homeowners into paying for unnecessary or poor-quality roofing work took more than £1m from victims, according to National Trading Standards. Twelve members received prison sentences totalling more than 63 years; the ringleader, Frederick Finney, was jailed for six years and nine months.

segments.title: A family’s account
segments.body: Nicola Lamb says her father, Michael Cooper, paid the gang £61,000 after being approached at home. She says he was shocked when trading standards told him he may have been defrauded. Cooper, who had recently received an early Alzheimer’s diagnosis, died in October 2025; his daughter says she cannot separate the effects of the illness from the distress of the fraud.

segments.title: Avoiding doorstep fraud
segments.body: Citizens Advice says suspected roofing scams were the most common fraud handled by its consumer service last year, and that 77% involved doorstep sales. It advises people to be wary of unsolicited offers, seek references and get agreed work in writing. Consumers may have 14 days to cancel work agreed in their home.

content.headline: England plans £100 fines for loud music on buses
content.shortHeadline: Bus passengers in England could face £100 fines for loud music
content.standfirst: New guidance will let local authorities fine bus passengers who refuse to stop nuisance behaviour. A separate campaign will ask rail passengers to use headphones, though transport groups question how the rules will be enforced.

sources.originalTitle: People playing loud music on buses could face £100 fine
Andy Burnham launches campaign against ‘headphone dodgers’ on public transport

segments.body: Bus passengers in England could face fines of up to £100 for loud music, vaping, littering or threatening behaviour if they refuse to comply with a request to stop. New guidance will explain how local authorities can use powers introduced earlier this year.

segments.title: Enforcement questions
segments.body: The government says bus drivers will not enforce the rules; authorised officers or police will. Rail passengers are also being urged to use headphones in a national campaign. Transport groups and opposition politicians have questioned whether there will be enough officers to make the rules effective.

Transport Focus says its research found four in 10 passengers felt vulnerable because of antisocial behaviour. A transport union welcomed action on nuisance behaviour but said ministers should also address violence and abuse against passengers and workers.

content.headline: Blood tests show possible IBD warning signs years before diagnosis
content.shortHeadline: Blood patterns may signal IBD years before diagnosis
content.standfirst: Researchers found different antibody patterns in blood samples from people who later developed Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis. The findings are not a clinical test and need confirmation in other groups.

sources.originalTitle: Warning signs could predict inflammatory bowel disease a decade before diagnosis

segments.body: A study of blood samples from US military personnel found antibody patterns linked to Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis up to a decade before diagnosis. The researchers say the immune system may show warning signs before symptoms appear.

segments.title: Not a test for patients yet
segments.body: The patterns differed between the two forms of inflammatory bowel disease. The study shows an association, not that the antibodies or infections caused the conditions, and the results need to be checked in other populations. Researchers say the method remains a research tool, not a test ready for clinical use.

If confirmed, earlier detection could help doctors identify people at risk before inflammation damages the gut. An independent gastroenterology professor called the findings an important insight but cautioned that the techniques are not yet ready for routine care.

content.headline: Søren Gade quits parliament, citing Venstre split and disputed profile
content.shortHeadline: Søren Gade quits parliament over party divisions
content.standfirst: The former defence minister says he can no longer support Venstre’s direction, particularly over a contested agricultural law. He also cited a newspaper profile based on anonymous sources as part of his decision.

image.caption: Søren Gade, who has announced he is leaving the Folketing.

sources.originalTitle: Søren Gade stopper i Folketinget
Troels Lund Poulsen er "ærgerlig" over Gades afgang – men hovedpinen er ikke ovre

segments.body: Søren Gade, a former Danish defence minister and speaker of parliament, says he is leaving the Folketing. In a Facebook post, he named internal disagreement over Venstre’s direction on a law regulating agricultural nitrogen emissions as the main reason.

segments.title: A difficult departure
segments.body: Gade also cited a Jyllands-Posten profile about him, which relied on anonymous sources and was published on the day he left the speaker’s role. He said he felt he had been personally torn apart and was distressed by the possibility that former colleagues had contributed to it.

Venstre leader Troels Lund Poulsen said he was sorry to see Gade go. Danish commentators described the departure as another blow for a party facing internal divisions. Gade said he hoped Erik Flyvholm would take over his parliamentary seat; the gather does not confirm who will succeed him.

content.headline: Wolt’s alcohol block failed to stop orders for a customer seeking help
content.shortHeadline: Wolt’s alcohol-exclusion system failed to block orders
content.standfirst: A woman who asked Wolt to block her from buying alcohol was still able to order vodka from some shops. The company apologised and says it is investigating why the restriction failed.

image.caption: Jens says Wolt deliveries of alcohol continued despite his partner’s request to be excluded.

sources.originalTitle: Wolt henviste til udelukkelsesordning: Misbruger kan stadig få vodka bragt til døren

segments.body: A woman in Fredericia who asked Wolt to exclude her from buying alcohol was still able to order vodka through the delivery app, according to DR. Her partner says two orders arrived after Wolt support confirmed she had been added to the exclusion system; DR says it reviewed the correspondence and order evidence.

segments.title: Company response
segments.body: Wolt apologised to the customer, saying the restriction had not worked as intended and that it was investigating the failure. The restriction did block alcohol purchases from one shop, but not others, DR reports. Wolt did not explain in detail how its exclusion system works.

The woman had previously described how easy alcohol delivery could make it to relapse. Alcohol & Society told DR that ready access to alcohol can affect people with addiction and said it would pay closer attention to delivery services. The customer’s partner called for a more reliable system.

content.headline: Lundbeck nominates former Novo Nordisk chief Lars Fruergaard as chair
content.shortHeadline: Lars Fruergaard nominated to chair Lundbeck
content.standfirst: Lundbeck has nominated Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen, Novo Nordisk’s former chief executive, to become its chair. The appointment depends on shareholder approval at the company’s annual meeting.

image.caption: Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen has been nominated to chair Lundbeck.

sources.originalTitle: Lars Fruergaard scorer nyt job

segments.body: Lars Fruergaard Jørgensen has been nominated to become chair of Danish pharmaceutical company Lundbeck, according to a company announcement reported by DR. He is due to join the board as an observer on 10 November.

The proposed appointment follows the announcement that current chair Dorothea Wenzel is stepping down. Fruergaard worked at Novo Nordisk from 1991 to 2025, including as its chief executive. Shareholders must approve his appointment at Lundbeck’s annual meeting in the spring.

content.headline: Study offers clues to why large dogs age faster than small dogs
content.shortHeadline: Study finds cellular ageing differences in large and small dogs
content.standfirst: Blood samples from nearly 900 dogs point to differences in how cells change with age, with some potentially harmful activity appearing earlier in larger dogs. Researchers do not yet know why the breeds differ.

image.caption: A dog, illustrating research into how ageing differs between large and small breeds.

sources.originalTitle: Forskere finder mulig forklaring på, hvorfor små hunde lever længere end store

segments.body: Researchers studying blood samples from nearly 900 dogs found signs of cellular ageing that appeared earlier in larger dogs than in smaller ones. The research, published in Science, offers a possible clue to why large dogs tend to have shorter lives.

The study found increased activity in parts of the DNA associated with genetic errors among large dogs, which may help explain their higher risk of some diseases, including cancer. Researchers also saw a possible difference between male and female dogs, but could not explain it.

The findings do not establish why size is linked to lifespan, or prove that the observed cellular changes cause earlier disease. A veterinary professor told DR the research could help explain why large breeds develop cancer earlier in life.

content.headline: Researchers drop leap seconds; a leap hour may be needed far in the future
content.shortHeadline: Leap seconds to end as timekeepers allow for a possible leap hour
content.standfirst: International timekeepers have decided to stop adding leap seconds from next year, citing risks to systems that depend on precise time. A leap hour could eventually be used instead, though likely not for more than 1,000 years.

image.caption: An illustration of Earth, whose changing rotation has prompted a new approach to timekeeping.

sources.originalTitle: Forskere har skrottet skudsekundet. Nu kan en skudtime blive nødvendig om tusinder af år

segments.body: Researchers and diplomats at an international timekeeping conference have decided to stop adding leap seconds from next year. Since 1972, 27 seconds have been added to Coordinated Universal Time to keep it roughly aligned with Earth’s rotation.

segments.title: Why the change
segments.body: Earth’s rotation varies, and has sped up since the mid-2010s. Timekeepers feared the need for a first-ever negative leap second, which could disrupt computer systems and infrastructure that depend on precise time. The new approach accepts a larger gap between official time and Earth’s rotation.

A leap hour could be introduced if the difference eventually approaches an hour, but the report says it is likely to be more than 1,000 years before that is necessary. Researchers say the change preserves the link between the global time standard and Earth’s rotation while reducing the risk of technical disruption.

content.headline: Danish YouTuber’s investigative video restored after defamation complaint
content.shortHeadline: YouTube restores Danish creator’s video after complaint
content.standfirst: A video by creator Oliver Hvam was unavailable for more than a day after YouTube received a defamation complaint. The dispute raises questions about the role and responsibilities of independent online news creators.

image.caption: Danish YouTube creator Oliver Hvam, known online as Bruhliver.

sources.originalTitle: 300.000 fulgte med i youtubers projekt – men så gik skærmen i sort

segments.body: A YouTube video by Oliver Hvam, whose channel is known as Bruhliver, was taken offline after the platform received a complaint alleging defamation. The video, part of his investigative series Kortlagt, had nearly 300,000 views in a few days and was restored on Wednesday after being unavailable for more than a day.

segments.title: An emerging media role
segments.body: Hvam says his two-person team spends months researching each report and follows press ethics. Media analyst Camilla Mehlsen says creators such as Hvam can reach younger audiences and compete with traditional media for attention.

Mehlsen says public funding for news influencers would require comparable standards of accountability and oversight, including an editor responsible for the content. TV 2 says it sought comment from the restaurateur whom Hvam believes made the complaint but did not receive a response before publication.

content.headline: Cleaner accidentally locked in Copenhagen court cell for three days
content.shortHeadline: Cleaner found after three days locked in Copenhagen court cell
content.standfirst: A cleaner became trapped in a basement cell in a former Østre Landsret building after its door closed behind her. She was found after her husband raised the alarm, according to the reports.

image.caption: A basement cell door at the former Østre Landsret building where a cleaner was trapped.

sources.originalTitle: Kvinde fundet bag smækket dør efter tre døgn
Rengøringsansat blev ved et uheld låst inde i celle i tre døgn

segments.body: A cleaner was accidentally locked inside a basement cell in a former Østre Landsret building on Bredgade in Copenhagen in September. The cell door could not be opened from inside, and she had no phone with her. She was found and helped out after three days.

segments.title: How she was found
segments.body: Her husband went looking for her after she failed to return home and spotted her bicycle near the building. He called police, who found her and took her to hospital. The building is now used intermittently by Copenhagen City Court and can otherwise be empty.
The court and the cleaner’s employer, Coor, confirmed the incident. The reports say she was offered crisis support and later returned to work. Coor did not provide further comment to TV 2.

content.headline: Vestervig group marks 20 years of efforts to revive the village
content.shortHeadline: Vestervig marks 20 years of work to tackle derelict homes
content.standfirst: A local group says it has helped demolish 29 derelict houses and renovate others over two decades. Vestervig has lost residents, but members point to rising school numbers and new families as signs of improvement.

sources.originalTitle: 29 spøgelseshuse revet ned i landsby

segments.body: Vestervig Byfornyelse is marking 20 years of efforts to address abandoned and deteriorating homes in the Thy village. The locally organised group says 29 houses have been demolished, while others have been renovated and sold or rented to new residents.

segments.title: Beyond demolition
segments.body: The group says its work has also expanded to attracting services and residents. It recently helped bring two doctors to the village, who will work in former school premises. Members say the aim is to make Vestervig a more attractive place for families and new arrivals.

Vestervig’s population has fallen by 20% over the group’s two decades of work. A member says the trend may be turning, pointing to increasing school enrolment and families moving in; the report does not provide figures for those recent changes.

content.headline: Celtic hit Hearts for seven in a 7-1 derby demolition
content.shortHeadline: Celtic thrash Hearts 7-1 in Glasgow derby
content.standfirst: Celtic overwhelmed Hearts at Celtic Park, scoring seven in a one-sided derby. BBC Sport’s Tom English says Hearts’ attacking approach left them exposed, while Celtic will look to build on a statement win.

image.caption: Celtic score their fifth goal as Hearts defenders Stephen Kingsley and Jamie McCart try to stop them.

sources.originalTitle: Hearts roll out red carpet ... and Celtic walk all over it

segments.body:
Celtic beat Hearts 7-1 at Celtic Park after scoring twice inside the opening 10 minutes. Tom English’s match analysis says Hearts’ high defensive line and errors in possession left them vulnerable to Celtic’s pace, as the hosts repeatedly turned loose balls into chances and goals.

The scale of the defeat raises questions about Hearts’ away form and their ability to sustain a title challenge. English notes that Celtic, meanwhile, will need to use the result as fuel for the season ahead.

content.headline: Brighton beat Palace 5-0 as Sage admits he does not know his future
content.shortHeadline: Brighton thrash Palace 5-0; Sage unsure of his future
content.standfirst: Brighton scored five in a dominant derby win, including Diego Gomez’s strike from halfway. Palace manager Pierre Sage apologised for his team’s display and said he did not know whether he would be given time to turn things around.

image.caption: Brighton celebrate during their 5-0 win over Crystal Palace.

sources.originalTitle: Shades of Barca and Beckham - Brighton aim to maintain superb start
Sage feels 'shame' at Palace thrashing with future in doubt
Crystal Palace

segments.body:
Brighton swept Crystal Palace aside 5-0, scoring three times in the opening 10 minutes. Diego Gomez’s goal from 51 metres was the standout moment: the strike put Brighton 2-0 up and was the Premier League’s longest-range goal since 2017, according to the report. Brighton have now scored 23 league goals in seven matches and sit third.

Palace have conceded 17 goals in their opening seven league games, the most in the division. Sage took responsibility for the performance and apologised to supporters; asked if he would get time to improve the team, he said he did not know.

perspectives.body: Sage called the performance a source of “shame” and said the team had shown its “worst face”. He accepted responsibility as coach, but gave no assurance about whether he would be given time to address the problems.

content.headline: Man Utd extend winless run to six games after 1-1 draw at Leeds
content.shortHeadline: Man Utd held by Leeds as winless run reaches six
content.standfirst: Bryan Mbeumo scored again for Manchester United, but Dominic Calvert-Lewin’s equaliser left Michael Carrick’s side with just one point at Elland Road. It is United’s longest winless run since 2018-19.

image.caption: Manchester United players regroup during their 1-1 draw at Leeds.

sources.originalTitle: Mbeumo offers Carrick solace as Man Utd winless run goes on

segments.body:
Manchester United drew 1-1 at Leeds, extending their winless run to six matches. Mbeumo scored his fourth league goal in seven games, but Calvert-Lewin levelled shortly after half-time. United finished the match 13th in the table, with their position still liable to change as the round continues.

Carrick said the team had to accept the situation and work through it, while insisting he believes they can start a good run. The report also points to continued uncertainty in the side: Lisandro Martinez went off at half-time with a thigh injury, and United have used five different players at left-back this season.

content.headline: Madueke’s late goal gives Arsenal a narrow win at Nottingham Forest
content.shortHeadline: Madueke strikes late as Arsenal edge Forest
content.standfirst: Noni Madueke came off the bench to score the only goal in a tight match at the City Ground. The win gives Arsenal three points in their title defence and adds to the winger’s recent run of strong performances.

image.caption: Noni Madueke celebrates after scoring the winner for Arsenal against Nottingham Forest.

sources.originalTitle: Madueke's 'anger and conviction' shows he's more than a 'finisher'

segments.body:
Arsenal beat Nottingham Forest 1-0 after Madueke scored in the 80th minute. Introduced at half-time, he cut inside and hit a shot that took a deflection on its way in. Arsenal had struggled to create clear chances before the goal.

Madueke has started only one Premier League game this season, but has produced three good performances in a row, according to the report. Mikel Arteta praised his growing decisiveness and said Arsenal’s substitutes have contributed more Premier League goals than any other side since the start of last season.

content.headline: Kartal loses Wuhan final but will become British number one
content.shortHeadline: Kartal falls in Wuhan final but rises to British number one
content.standfirst: Sonay Kartal’s remarkable return from a six-month injury absence ended in defeat by Maja Chwalinska, but the run to the Wuhan final will lift her to 50th in the rankings and make her Britain’s number one.

image.caption: Sonay Kartal, who is set to become British number one when the rankings are released on Monday.

sources.originalTitle: Britain's Kartal misses out on biggest title of her career

segments.body:
Sonay Kartal lost the Wuhan Open final 2-6 6-4 6-2 to Maja Chwalinska after leading by a break in the second set. Kartal, playing only her 10th match since returning from a six-month absence with a back injury, had won the first set before her opponent turned the match around.

The week still brings a major ranking milestone: Kartal is set to rise to 50th in the world and become British number one when the rankings are published on Monday. She reached the final after beating several notable opponents, including former major champions and current top-10 players.

content.headline: Toulouse survive Exeter’s challenge as Northampton claim English rugby’s sole U
content.shortHeadline: Toulouse edge Exeter; Northampton earn English rugby’s only win
content.standfirst: Toulouse fought back with 14 players to beat Exeter in a Champions Cup thriller, while Northampton became the only English side to win in the opening round, edging Cardiff in a nervy contest.

sources.originalTitle: Toulouse deny Exeter famous Champions Cup victory
Northampton beat Cardiff for first English win

segments.title: Toulouse fight back
segments.body: Toulouse beat Exeter in a frenetic Champions Cup match despite playing with 14 men after Rodrigue Neti’s first-half red card. Exeter winger Zack Wimbush scored a hat-trick, but Toulouse pulled ahead late. Exeter had a chance to force a draw in the final seconds, but Henry Slade’s penalty went wide.

segments.title: Northampton get the English win
segments.body: Northampton were the only English team to win in the opening round, beating Cardiff at Franklin’s Gardens. Saints led 14-0 at half-time, but Cardiff fought back to make it 14-12 before George Hendy and Fraser Dingwall scored in the closing stages. Northampton won without securing a bonus point.

content.headline: Lisowski begins Northern Ireland Open defence as Selby exits
content.shortHeadline: Lisowski wins, but Selby suffers surprise NI Open exit
content.standfirst: Jack Lisowski opened his title defence with a 4-1 win in Belfast, but Mark Selby let a 2-0 lead slip and lost 4-2 to Louis Heathcote in the first round.

image.caption: Jack Lisowski, who began his Northern Ireland Open title defence with a win in Belfast.

sources.originalTitle: Selby out but Lisowski advances in NI Open defence

segments.body:
Reigning champion Jack Lisowski beat Huang Jiahao 4-1 to start his Northern Ireland Open defence. Lisowski raced into a 3-0 lead and clinched the deciding frame on the black. He will face Anthony McGill in the second round.

Four-time world champion Mark Selby was among the opening-day casualties. He led Heathcote 2-0 but lost four frames in a row. Former world champions Neil Robertson and Shaun Murphy also went out in the evening session.

content.headline: Chacarra wins in India to take the Race to Dubai lead
content.shortHeadline: Chacarra wins in India and moves top of Race to Dubai
content.standfirst: Eugenio Chacarra held off Daniel Hillier to win the DP World India Championship by two strokes. The Spaniard’s third DP World Tour victory of the season puts him top of the Race to Dubai with three events remaining.

image.caption: Eugenio Chacarra, winner of the DP World India Championship.

sources.originalTitle: Chacarra wins in India to take Race to Dubai lead

segments.body:
Eugenio Chacarra won the DP World India Championship by two strokes, finishing on 21 under. A nine-under 63 in his third round gave him a five-shot lead, and his final-round 70 was enough to hold off New Zealand’s Daniel Hillier, who birdied the last.

The victory is Chacarra’s third on the DP World Tour this season and moves him to the top of the Race to Dubai standings. Patrick Reed, who had led since March, finished tied for 23rd; Rory McIlroy was tied for 42nd. Three events remain before the season’s leading player is crowned.

content.headline: How Fontaines D.C. built a path from Dublin dive bars to stadiums
content.shortHeadline: Fontaines D.C.’s road from Dublin clubs to stadiums
content.standfirst: The Irish band’s ascent has come through ambitious records, relentless touring and champions on radio and in the industry—not a campaign built around viral moments. Their fifth album arrives as they prepare for a bigger stage.

image.caption: Fontaines D.C., with frontman Grian Chatten at the centre.

sources.originalTitle: ‘The mainstream has come to them’: how did Fontaines DC go from Dublin dive bars to headlining stadiums?

segments.body: Fontaines D.C. formed in Dublin in 2014 and built their following through small venues, steady songwriting and extensive touring. Their first album, Dogrel, reached the UK and Irish top 10 in 2019; now they are heading towards UK stadiums, US arenas and major festival slots, with a fifth album, Dopamine Chamber, arriving alongside that expansion.

segments.title: A less-is-more ascent
segments.body: People around the band point to early support from BBC Radio 6 Music, the label’s emphasis on authenticity and lyrics, and the decision to keep releasing music during lockdown. Music-industry observers also describe the band’s online following as organic rather than manufactured. The story’s contributors see no single explanation for the scale of the rise: talent, commitment, support and luck all played a part.

content.headline: Shygirl’s new album turns a love story toward rock and vulnerability
content.shortHeadline: Shygirl moves from club sounds to rock on Swallow!
content.standfirst: The London artist’s forthcoming album draws on a settled relationship and a new musical direction. She also reflects on the work behind her rise and the barriers she sees for women in the industry.

image.caption: Shygirl in 2026.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I need to prove my family’s sacrifice was worth it’: how pop auteur Shygirl slogged her way to the top

segments.body: Shygirl’s second album, Swallow!, moves away from the hyperpop, UK garage and electronic sounds of her earlier work towards an expansive, guitar-led rock record. She describes it as a response to intimacy and devotion, drawing on her relationship with actor George Smale and a new willingness to let vulnerability shape the songs.

segments.title: Ambition on her own terms
segments.body: Born Blane Muise, Shygirl describes growing up in south-east London with parents who worked a succession of jobs, and says their sacrifices drive her determination. After building a career from club music and leaving a secure day job, she has opened arenas for Beyoncé and Charli xcx. She says gender remains a significant barrier and wants to work with people who challenge the status quo.

content.headline: Fontaines D.C.’s Dopamine Chamber makes stadium rock feel unsettling
content.shortHeadline: Fontaines D.C. turn stadium rock dark on Dopamine Chamber
content.standfirst: The band’s fifth album pairs sleek, seductive rock with a bleak view of pleasure, technology and emotional numbness. This review hears beauty in the music, but little comfort.

sources.originalTitle: Dopamine Chamber

segments.body: Pitchfork hears Dopamine Chamber as a record about escape that refuses to offer reassurance. Its polished stadium rock draws listeners in even as Grian Chatten’s lyrics evoke compulsive pleasure, online dissociation and a society dulled by its own appetites.

segments.title: Beauty with a sting
segments.body: The review argues that the album’s glamour and pessimism depend on each other. Songs including “Marianne” and “Where Is Gone?” use alluring melodies and performances to make their darker ideas more unnerving; even the record’s portrait of romance suggests it can become another fleeting hit of pleasure.

content.headline: Soft Cell’s Danceteria becomes the duo’s final album after Dave Ball’s death
content.shortHeadline: Soft Cell’s final album is a bittersweet return to New York
content.standfirst: Marc Almond says he would not make another Soft Cell record without Dave Ball. Their completed album revisits the clubs and contradictions of early-1980s New York, now as a closing chapter.

image.caption: Marc Almond and Dave Ball of Soft Cell.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Soft Cell had agreed that Danceteria was finished; two days later, keyboardist Dave Ball died. Singer Marc Almond calls the release their sixth and final album, saying he would not continue the group without his longtime collaborator. The record looks back to the New York club scene that shaped them after the success of “Tainted Love.”

segments.title: The city behind the songs
segments.body: Almond describes the album as a love letter to a dangerous, creative city, while also recalling the loneliness and fear he witnessed as the AIDS crisis took hold. He says the pair grew closer while making the record and feels relieved they completed it together, though saddened Ball could not see its release.

content.headline: Tom Morello’s first solo rock album carries his activist convictions
content.shortHeadline: Tom Morello brings his activism to a solo rock album
content.standfirst: The Rage Against the Machine guitarist says his new record is a response to a dangerous political moment. He also recalls how his mother’s example shaped his belief in ordinary people’s power to act.

image.caption: Tom Morello.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Morello on Rage Against the Machine fans turning against him

segments.body: Tom Morello describes Everyone Gets What They Want as his first full-length solo rock album, built around anti-racist and anti-fascist songs. He presents it as a personal response to a global far-right resurgence and says he regards making rebellious rock as an act of resistance.

segments.title: A family inheritance
segments.body: Morello credits his mother, Mary, with instilling his politics. He recalls her taking part in civil-rights and labour causes and teaching him about the United Farm Workers’ grape boycott when he was a child. He says the belief that ordinary people can change the world runs through the music he has written.

content.headline: Spacemen 3’s The Perfect Prescription finds freedom in its rough edges
content.shortHeadline: The strange, searching pull of Spacemen 3’s The Perfect Prescription
content.standfirst: Pitchfork revisits the 1987 album as an unconventional meeting of drone, gospel feeling and guitar experiments. Its account finds the record compelling not because it perfects its ideas, but because it lets them remain ragged.

sources.originalTitle: The Perfect Prescription

segments.body: The Perfect Prescription is framed as Spacemen 3’s defining record: a guitar album that redirects attention from conventional rhythm towards repetition, texture and atmosphere. The review traces its mix of indie rock, drone, heavy psychedelia and spiritual influence, and argues that the music still sounds strange because it resists tidy resolution.

segments.title: Accident and intention
segments.body: The piece resists treating the album as a perfectly plotted trip. It describes long sessions, improvised techniques and musical ideas that sometimes emerged by chance, while also noting the record’s bleak account of drug use. Its lasting force, the reviewer suggests, lies in the tension between ecstatic sound and the loneliness beneath it.

content.headline: A Tate Britain exhibition revisits the unruly energy of 1990s culture
content.shortHeadline: The images and boundary-crossing spirit of 1990s Britain
content.standfirst: A new exhibition brings together photographs of fashion, music, clubs and street life. Its curator argues that the decade’s cultural shifts were also about who got to participate and whose voices were heard.

sources.originalTitle: 'Rock 'n' roll swagger': 10 iconic images capturing the chaotic energy of '90s Brit culture

segments.body: The BBC’s tour of Tate Britain’s The 90s: Art & Fashion moves through images of club nights, models, artists, musicians and young people out after dark. Together they evoke a decade in which music, fashion and visual art frequently crossed paths, with a restless, often contradictory energy.

segments.title: Who gets to make culture?
segments.body: Curator Edward Enninful says the period is remembered not only for its styles but for changes in who could take part and be heard. Photographers featured in the exhibition recall club scenes and informal gatherings where people made their own spaces; Enninful sees the decade’s influence as still unfolding.

content.headline: How ? and the Mysterians turned “96 Tears” into a garage-rock landmark
content.shortHeadline: The unlikely rise and long afterlife of “96 Tears”
content.standfirst: A home-recorded single by a young Mexican-American band reached the top of the US charts in 1966. Its rough-edged sound later helped shape garage rock and punk.

sources.originalTitle: 'A hypnotic effect that fills you with joy': The incredible story of 96 Tears, the US's unlikeliest one-hit wonder

segments.body: Recorded in a small Bay City studio and released by a local label, “96 Tears” became a US number one for ? and the Mysterians. The BBC traces the song from its organ riff and teen heartbreak lyrics to the band’s DIY route through local radio and, eventually, national distribution.

segments.title: A life beyond the charts
segments.body: The band did not repeat the single’s success, but the track found a second life through garage-rock revivals and later musicians who took inspiration from its raw sound. The article places the group in a regional Mexican-American music community and explains how the song’s afterlife grew well beyond its brief chart peak.

content.headline: Masterplan review: Stanley Tucci’s Louvre heist caper has a few tricks
content.shortHeadline: Masterplan’s heist tricks can’t rescue its thin story
content.standfirst: The Amazon thriller gives Stanley Tucci a chance to send up a suave criminal mastermind, but its family revelations and overextended plot keep it from making much of an impression.

image.caption: Stanley Tucci in Masterplan.

sources.originalTitle: Masterplan review – Stanley Tucci is wasted in Amazon’s smooth-brained heist caper

segments.body: In Masterplan, two young criminals are recruited by veteran thief Roger, played by Stanley Tucci, for an elaborate scheme to steal the Mona Lisa. The film offers double-crosses, gadgets and some enjoyable heist mechanics, including a clever use of a helium balloon, but its characters are too thinly drawn to give the caper much emotional weight.

The Guardian review finds Tucci game for the comedy and director Thomas Vincent effective when the film sticks to espionage. But the story’s increasingly ridiculous turns and unnecessary length leave it as forgettable streaming entertainment rather than a satisfying star vehicle.

content.headline: NAZA review: anonymous Israeli intelligence testimony casts a shadow over Gaza
content.shortHeadline: NAZA’s anonymous testimony makes for a chilling Gaza film
content.standfirst: Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary presents claims by Israeli intelligence personnel about how strikes are planned. Its anonymity limits the testimony’s impact, but the film’s account is deeply unsettling.

image.caption: Tel Aviv at night, as seen in NAZA.

sources.originalTitle: NAZA review – Israeli intelligence officers cast chilling light on civilian deaths

segments.body: NAZA uses interviews with Israeli intelligence personnel whose faces and voices are concealed. They allege that surveillance and AI-assisted systems help identify targets in Gaza, and describe projected civilian deaths as part of strike planning. These are claims made by the anonymous interviewees; the review notes that their anonymity also makes their testimony harder to assess.

segments.title: A disturbing distance
segments.body: The Guardian critic describes the film’s night-time rooftop setting in Tel Aviv as a striking contrast to the accounts of violence in Gaza. The documentary also includes testimony about military operations in northern Gaza and attacks on civilians seeking food. The review cautions against a speaker’s comparison with Nazism, while finding the film’s focus on civilian harm powerful.

content.headline: La Bola Negra connects three gay lives across a century of Spanish history
content.shortHeadline: La Bola Negra traces gay desire and history across Spain
content.standfirst: Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s film moves between 1932, 1937 and 2017, joining stories of desire, persecution and family memory. Its festival reception has fuelled awards speculation, but the film’s ambition is the stronger story.

sources.originalTitle: 'Immediately spellbinding': Four reasons why gay Spanish epic La Bola Negra could win the Oscar for best picture

segments.body: La Bola Negra follows three gay men across different periods of Spanish history: a soldier during the Civil War, a young man excluded from an elite club in 1932, and a historian in 2017. The film draws inspiration from Federico García Lorca while building its own stories around memory, sexual repression and the inheritance of family history.

segments.title: A form as expansive as its subject
segments.body: The BBC highlights the film’s shifting visual styles, its ensemble performances and its blend of historical drama, romance and family story. It reports that the film won the audience award at Toronto and has attracted awards attention; predictions about a best-picture nomination remain just that, rather than a settled outcome.

content.headline: Artificial turns OpenAI’s founding into a drama about who controls AI
content.shortHeadline: Artificial dramatises the fight over OpenAI’s future
content.standfirst: Luca Guadagnino’s film follows the growing divide between Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever. The BBC reads it as a cautionary story about AI safety and commercial power, while noting that the fictionalised characters are not equally developed.

sources.originalTitle: AI fears are growing – and unsettling new film Artificial puts them, and the future of humanity, centre stage

segments.body: Artificial traces OpenAI’s development from a nonprofit venture to the company behind ChatGPT, focusing on the conflict between co-founders Sam Altman and Ilya Sutskever. The film puts questions about AI safety, secrecy and commercial interests at the centre of a story about who gets to shape the technology’s future.

segments.title: A timely but uneven warning
segments.body: The BBC says the film’s imagined scenario of AI evading a human test resonates with recent concerns raised about autonomous systems, but describes the timing as fortunate rather than prophetic. It also notes that Sutskever receives a fuller portrayal than Altman, whose motives remain less explored.

content.headline: What makes a film adaptation work? It may be the freedom to change the book
content.shortHeadline: Great film adaptations often know when to leave books behind
content.standfirst: A writer surveying adaptations from The Shining to Trainspotting argues that fidelity is no guarantee of success. The most effective films find a visual language of their own.

image.caption: A collage featuring The Shining, The Godfather and The Silence of the Lambs.

sources.originalTitle: An open book: how to make a great film adaptation, from The Shining to Trainspotting

segments.body: The essay challenges the idea that a successful film must be faithful to its source. Great novels can produce great films, and weaker books can still become effective screen stories; what matters is how a filmmaker translates the material from words into images, sound and performance.

segments.title: Adaptation as reinvention
segments.body: Examples including Children of Men, Orlando and The Shining illustrate the case for taking liberties rather than assembling a reverent list of a novel’s best-known scenes. The writer also acknowledges that there is no single version of a book in every reader’s mind, making fidelity an uncertain measure in the first place.

content.headline: Case 137 review: a police-brutality inquiry tests one officer’s loyalties
content.shortHeadline: Case 137 follows a police officer investigating police violence
content.standfirst: Dominik Moll’s procedural follows an internal-affairs officer tracing the source of a protester’s injuries. Its painstaking investigation is compelling, though the film’s conflicts do not reach the complexity it promises.

image.caption: Léa Drucker in Dossier 137.

sources.originalTitle: Case 137 review – tense gilets-jaunes thriller divides cop’s loyalties over police brutality

segments.body: In Case 137, Léa Drucker plays Stéphanie, an officer investigating injuries to a teenage protester during France’s 2018 gilets jaunes demonstrations. The inquiry turns personal when she discovers the boy is from her hometown, pushing her to pursue evidence while risking accusations that she is cutting corners herself.

The review finds the film strongest as Stéphanie and her colleagues painstakingly trace CCTV and phone footage to identify the officers involved. Its larger tensions—between police and critics, and between Paris and a left-behind provincial town—are less fully developed, but the film remains valuable in its attention to accountability.

content.headline: Ellie and Natasia bring new life experience to their sketch-show return
content.shortHeadline: Ellie and Natasia return with a changed view of their characters
content.standfirst: The comedians behind Ellie & Natasia are parents now, like some of the mothers they once spoofed. They discuss that shift, the show’s new sketches and the challenge of finding shared cultural references online.

image.caption: Natasia Demetriou and Ellie White in Ellie & Natasia.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It was like your worst nightmare’ – Ellie and Natasia on mums, music … and failing to make Bob Mortimer smile

segments.body: Ellie White and Natasia Demetriou return for a second series of their sketch show after becoming mothers themselves. They say that experience has given them a new empathy for characters such as their hygiene-obsessed mums, though they were careful not to make pregnancy the focus of the series.

segments.title: Comedy in an endless feed
segments.body: The pair have shifted away from specific musical parodies towards sketches about social-media formats, from day-in-the-life videos to visual podcasts. They say the internet makes it harder to find a shared reference everyone recognises—and sometimes a real online creator has already done the joke.

content.headline: Last One Laughing: Halloween adds screams to its no-laughing challenge
content.shortHeadline: Last One Laughing tests comedians’ poker faces with screams
content.standfirst: The Halloween special asks its comics to suppress screams as well as laughter. Its participants describe the strange pressures of the format and the careful production behind the apparent chaos.

image.caption: Daisy May Cooper on Last One Laughing: Halloween.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I didn’t know I was a screamer. Turns out I am’ – the spooky secrets of Last One Laughing: Halloween

segments.body: For the Halloween special of Last One Laughing, comedians must keep a straight face and avoid screaming while trying to make their competitors do either. Phil Wang says he discovered he was a screamer; host Jimmy Carr argues that jokes and jump scares draw on a similar element of surprise.

segments.title: A game built in the edit
segments.body: Contestants describe the long, exhausting hours and the effort needed to hold back two different reactions. Carr and Wang also point to the show’s challenges, props and close monitoring of every contestant; the footage, Carr says, can reveal moments even the people in the room did not notice.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s uncertain future leaves fans asking when it will return
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain pause after its latest series
content.standfirst: The BBC’s partnership with Disney+ has ended, a planned Christmas special has been cancelled and no new Doctor has been announced. Fans and television voices disagree on what the long-running series needs next.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Jodie Whittaker and Ncuti Gatwa.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Since the latest series ended in 2025, Doctor Who has had no new episodes. The BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+, cancelled a planned Christmas special and put future production out to tender; no new Doctor has been announced. The article reports that the BBC has declined to comment further.

segments.title: A format built to change
segments.body: The feature traces the show’s history of renewal, from its 1963 debut and 1989 cancellation to its revival in 2005. Contributors point to changing showrunners, scripts and audience responses as part of its latest troubles, while lifelong fan Frank Skinner urges the BBC to bring it back without losing sight of its established identity.

content.headline: Time’s prison drama examines how anger and isolation shape young men
content.shortHeadline: Time shows the anger and isolation inside a young offenders’ prison
content.standfirst: Jimmy McGovern’s third series moves to a young offenders’ institution, where both inmates and guards are trapped in violent hierarchies. The review links that behaviour to isolation and a weakened prison system.

image.caption: David Tennant as prison officer Bobby Bailey in Time.

sources.originalTitle: Time picks up where Adolescence left off

segments.body: The third series of Time takes place in a young offenders’ institution, where boys and prison staff navigate a culture shaped by violence, fear and power. The review argues that the guards are not outside that culture: some use violence to control inmates or manage their own strained relationships.

segments.title: Anger in a system under strain
segments.body: The series connects the characters’ aggression to unmet needs for love and connection, as well as to a prison regime where isolation has replaced much of the education and training described by one officer. The review sees no easy answer in the drama, but makes a case that the conditions themselves help sustain the behaviour they punish.

content.headline: Penguin Colony turns an Antarctic expedition into a strange, searching game
content.shortHeadline: Penguin Colony is an uncanny Antarctic adventure
content.standfirst: This low-poly exploration game puts players in control of penguins gathering words as they follow an expedition into a landscape of Nazis and Lovecraftian horror. Its unsettling mix builds towards an argument against both.

image.caption: Penguin Colony, an Antarctic adventure by Origame Digital.

sources.originalTitle: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors

segments.body: Penguin Colony sends players waddling, swimming and gliding across Antarctica as they follow the trail of an expedition chasing an otherworldly presence. You can switch between penguins with different abilities; the game’s unusual collectibles are words, gathered as you explore the frozen landscape and its traces of human occupation.

segments.title: A disquieting landscape
segments.body: The review describes a world that shifts from huts and ice floes to enormous labyrinths and alien structures, layered with a scientist’s narration and disturbing scenes of Nazi collapse. It can be uneven in its controls and sound, but the critic praises its unsettling tone and conclusion, which challenges Lovecraft’s racism and Nazi brutality.

content.headline: Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake updates a classic without losing its shape
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time gets a 4K makeover on Switch 2
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s remake adds modern controls and a newly orchestrated soundtrack to the 1998 adventure. Its revised Link model may divide players, but the hands-on preview finds the game’s structure still holds up.

image.caption: Link in the Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era

segments.body: The Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time gives Link a sprint, a manual jump, a movable camera and a streamlined inventory, alongside a more detailed Hyrule and newly orchestrated music. The preview finds the changes make the familiar adventure feel different under the controls while leaving its traditional dungeons and puzzles intact.

segments.title: A new look for an old world
segments.body: The preview sees Link’s glossy, doll-like appearance as the most contentious change. It raises the possibility that the design draws on Japanese puppet theatre, but notes that Nintendo has not explained its intentions. In motion, the reviewer finds the style coherent and sees no reason to conclude the game’s original identity has been ruined.

content.headline: Could independent arcades bring social gaming back to the high street?
content.shortHeadline: A new wave of arcades could make gaming social again
content.standfirst: After years of sprawling games built to hold players’ time, a columnist sees renewed interest in shorter arcade-style experiences. Small venues may offer something big publishers cannot: a local place to play together.

image.caption: A video game arcade.

sources.originalTitle: Ready player one? Why the games arcade is having a rebirth

segments.body: The article argues that players are tiring of games designed to demand endless time and attention, and points to a growing interest in contained, arcade-inspired experiences. It sees an opportunity for independent venues that curate new and classic games rather than simply offering coin-ops alongside drinks.

segments.title: More than a cabinet
segments.body: Games journalist Will Freeman says that a handful of small venues are taking an approach closer to independent bookshops and record stores, including a London café focused on imported Japanese arcade machines. The appeal is not only the games, but the chance to meet other players, learn from them and build a local community.

content.headline: A £350 GTA 6 collector’s box raises questions about who can afford gaming
content.shortHeadline: The GTA 6 collector’s box puts gaming’s rising costs in view
content.standfirst: Rockstar’s merchandise box costs £350 and does not include the game. The writer sees it as part of a wider divide between accessible mobile play and premium console gaming.

image.caption: The Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection.

sources.originalTitle: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming

segments.body: Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI collector’s box costs £350 and contains merchandise, but not the game or a download code. Buying both the box and the listed £70 game would bring the total to £420. The writer does not object to collecting, but notes that the price is unusually high.

segments.title: A widening spending divide
segments.body: The article connects the box to rising console and game prices, arguing that premium gaming increasingly depends on disposable income. It contrasts that market with mobile games, which reach a much larger share of players at little or no cost, and worries that the kinds of expansive games the writer values are becoming harder to access.

content.headline: Japan prepares a first mission to bring samples back from a Martian moon
content.shortHeadline: Japan plans first sample-return mission to a Martian moon
content.standfirst: The five-year mission aims to collect soil from Phobos and return it to Earth, where researchers hope it can help resolve how Mars’s two small moons formed. The launch is planned for Tuesday.

image.caption: Phobos photographed by Nasa’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.

sources.originalTitle: Japan to launch world-first mission to collect samples from Martian moon

segments.body: Japan’s space agency, Jaxa, is aiming to launch the Martian Moons eXploration mission on an H3 rocket. If successful, it will be the first mission to bring samples back from Phobos, one of Mars’s two small moons. The spacecraft is expected to reach the Mars region in 2027 and return its samples to Earth in 2031.

segments.title: What researchers hope to learn
segments.body: Scientists disagree on whether Phobos and Deimos formed from debris after an impact on Mars or are captured asteroids. Jaxa hopes analysis of Phobos soil will help settle the question. The mission will also observe Deimos and collect data that may help assess the moons’ possible use in future Mars exploration.

content.headline: Warming is raising the risk of turbulence pilots cannot see
content.shortHeadline: Climate change raises the risk of invisible air turbulence
content.standfirst: Clear-air turbulence can hit at cruising altitude without showing on radar. Researchers have found it has increased over recent decades, while pilots and airlines are testing new ways to forecast and respond to the danger.

image.caption: Turbulence can injure passengers and crew when they are not secured in their seats.

sources.originalTitle: Hiding in plane sight: the invisible turbulence that can strike out of a clear blue sky

segments.body: Turbulence caused by storms is often visible on radar; clear-air turbulence is not. It commonly occurs near jet streams, where changes in wind speed or direction can jolt an aircraft. An analysis of atmospheric data from 1979 to 2020 found severe clear-air turbulence increased by 55%, with moderate and light turbulence also rising.

segments.title: Forecasts and precautions
segments.body: Researchers say warming can intensify wind shear and add energy to thunderstorms, increasing turbulence risks. Airlines share sensor reports to improve near-term forecasts, and some are exploring lidar to detect conditions ahead. The article stresses that injuries often happen when people are not buckled in; aircraft are built to withstand far more turbulence than passengers can.

content.headline: World timekeepers vote to replace leap seconds with leap hours
content.shortHeadline: Leap seconds to give way to leap hours in timekeeping change
content.standfirst: The change is intended to reduce the risk of timing errors disrupting computer systems and infrastructure. Coordinated universal time may drift by as much as an hour before a correction is needed—a prospect the report says is thousands of years away.

image.caption: A clock at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, through which the prime meridian passes.

sources.originalTitle: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour

segments.body: Delegates from 69 countries have voted to move away from leap seconds, which are added to keep official time aligned with Earth’s irregular rotation. The new approach allows coordinated universal time to drift farther from astronomical time before a correction is made, avoiding a sudden 61- or 59-second minute.

segments.title: Why the system is changing
segments.body: Atomic clocks underpin systems including communications, navigation and electricity grids, but Earth’s rotation varies. Past leap-second adjustments have caused some computer systems to freeze or go offline; a negative leap second would be untested. The report says the first leap-hour adjustment is not expected for thousands of years.

content.headline: Margaret Hamilton, Apollo software pioneer, dies aged 90
content.shortHeadline: Apollo software pioneer Margaret Hamilton dies aged 90
content.standfirst: Hamilton led the MIT team that developed software for the Apollo Guidance Computer. Her preparation helped mission controllers respond to alarms during Apollo 11’s lunar landing without aborting the mission.

image.caption: Margaret Hamilton beside a model of the Apollo command module at MIT in 1969.

sources.originalTitle: Margaret Hamilton obituary

segments.body: Margaret Hamilton directed the software engineering division at MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory, which developed the computer systems used in Apollo. During Apollo 11’s descent, alarms prompted discussion of an abort. Hamilton recognised a problem she had rehearsed in simulations: a radar switch had been left active. Mission controllers reassured the crew, and the Eagle landed safely.

segments.title: A lasting contribution
segments.body: Hamilton was the first woman programmer on the Apollo project and led a team of about 100. She insisted on repeatedly testing software for faults, work the obituary says helped missions avoid known software bugs. She also coined the term “software engineering” to describe the discipline and its responsibilities.

content.headline: UK’s early flu season prompts calls for eligible people to get vaccinated
content.shortHeadline: Early flu rise prompts UK vaccination advice
content.standfirst: Flu infections remain relatively low but are rising earlier than usual, health officials say. Experts caution that an early start does not by itself mean a worse season, and explain how flu differs from common colds.

image.caption: Respiratory viruses can rise as the UK enters the colder months.

sources.originalTitle: Why so many people are sick right now

segments.body: Flu activity is rising in the UK earlier than usual, though rates remain relatively low, according to the UK Health Security Agency. Experts say the timing and severity of flu seasons vary, and an early start does not necessarily predict a worse winter. The agency is urging people eligible for an NHS flu vaccine to get it as soon as possible.

segments.title: How flu differs from a cold
segments.body: Flu usually comes on quickly, over hours, and is more likely to cause a raised temperature, fever and muscle aches. Colds more often bring a runny nose, sneezing, cough and sore throat, though symptoms can overlap. Experts say the reasons respiratory viruses peak in winter are still debated.

content.headline: Study finds high blood pressure in many UK adults under 40
content.shortHeadline: Study finds undetected high blood pressure among under-40s
content.standfirst: An analysis of a large UK study found high blood pressure in 15% of participants aged 18 to 39. Researchers say younger adults at risk may go unchecked under current NHS health-check arrangements.

image.caption: A blood-pressure check can be requested at a GP practice or pharmacy.

sources.originalTitle: The ‘silent killer’ blood pressure problem that affects under-40s too

segments.body: The study, drawing on measurements from 1.4 million UK adults, found that a third had high blood pressure; six in 10 of that group were unaware of it.
