Among participants aged 18 to 39, 15% had high blood pressure. The researchers caution that readings taken in a study may not reflect measurements taken at home while fully relaxed.

segments.title: How to get checked
segments.body: NHS heart-health checks are offered from age 40, but people can ask a GP or pharmacist for a blood-pressure measurement sooner. The experts quoted advise using a standard arm-cuff monitor rather than relying on phone apps or wearable devices, which they say have not generally been shown to be as accurate.

content.headline: German police detain Russian man linked to London hospital cyberattack
content.shortHeadline: Russian man detained over London hospital cyberattack
content.standfirst: The BBC says German investigators are examining whether the accused Qilin gang member was involved in the 2024 Synnovis attack, which disrupted blood testing at London hospitals. The case is also being examined for possible links to a patient’s death.

image.caption: The alleged Qilin gang member was detained by German police on arrival in Frankfurt.

sources.originalTitle: Russian man linked to deadly London hospitals hack arrested

segments.body: German police have detained a 28-year-old Russian man, identified by German media as Vladimir K., whom authorities accuse of being a core member of the Qilin cyber-crime gang. The BBC reports that German investigators have included the 2024 hack of Synnovis in their inquiry. The suspect has not been convicted.

segments.title: The impact of the attack
segments.body: The Synnovis ransomware attack disrupted pathology services at London hospitals, led to cancelled operations and diverted emergency patients, and affected more than 10,000 appointments. One hospital trust said a patient died unexpectedly after a long wait for a blood-test result, among several contributing factors. British police are examining whether their inquiry could lead to an unlawful-killing case.

content.headline: Austrian MEP urges EU action after nude deepfakes target women in politics
content.shortHeadline: MEP calls for EU action on sexualised deepfakes
content.standfirst: Lena Schilling says digitally altered nude images of her were circulated without consent. A report cited in the article found 50 MEPs had been targeted, most of them women, prompting calls to enforce an upcoming EU ban.

image.caption: Austrian MEP Lena Schilling says sexualised deepfakes of her were shared without her consent.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I felt disgusted’: MEP speaks out over nude deepfakes and urges EU action

segments.body: Austrian Green MEP Lena Schilling says she felt disgusted after finding nude deepfakes made from images of her at a press conference. A report by the Berlin-based thinktank Agora Digitale Transformation says 50 MEPs—46 women—have been targeted by sexualised deepfakes. Schilling calls the images digital violence and says they can discourage women from entering public life.

segments.title: A ban and questions about enforcement
segments.body: Schilling and German Green MEP Terry Reintke led a letter signed by 119 MEPs urging the EU to pair a ban on AI undressing apps and websites, scheduled to take effect on 2 December, with effective enforcement. Schilling says rules “on paper” will not protect people if loopholes allow the tools to keep operating.

content.headline: Rural Norfolk data-centre plan would use up to a gigawatt of power
content.shortHeadline: Norfolk data-centre plan raises power and land concerns
content.standfirst: A developer’s proposal near Tilney St Lawrence includes a data centre and solar farms across about 4,695 acres. Residents and local officials have raised concerns about water, construction traffic, nature and the site’s proximity to RAF Marham.

image.caption: Resident Sophie Pendrick says the proposed data-centre project has left her shocked by its scale.

sources.originalTitle: How has community reacted to major data centre plan?

segments.body: Evolution Power Limited proposes a data centre near Tilney St Lawrence in Fenland, Norfolk, with a maximum demand of one gigawatt of power. The plan also includes solar farms with a combined area of about 4,695 acres and up to 1.3 gigawatts of generating capacity. The developer says the project would support digital services and create jobs.

segments.title: Local concerns and next steps
segments.body: Residents have questioned the project’s scale, water use and construction traffic. The local council leader also raised concerns about nearby nature sites, roads and whether solar panels could affect RAF Marham. Because the proposal is classed as a nationally significant infrastructure project, the final decision rests with government; a public consultation is open until 26 November.

content.headline: Electronic noses help cities trace the source of industrial odours
content.shortHeadline: Cities use sensors to trace industrial odours
content.standfirst: Air monitors paired with weather data are helping officials identify which facilities may be responsible when bad smells prompt complaints. The approach offers evidence where odour rules are limited, though smell remains subjective.

image.caption: Newby Island landfill operators have been ordered to track odours with monitors and drones.

sources.originalTitle: Living with a stink? Technology might help

segments.body: In Des Moines, Iowa, a ring of monitors measures chemical compounds in the air alongside local weather conditions. Officials say the combined data can help trace an odour plume to a facility, replacing the earlier practice of driving to a complaint and sniffing the air. The city spends about $240,000 a year on the monitoring system.

segments.title: Monitoring is not the same as removing the smell
segments.body: In Milpitas, California, landfill operators have been ordered to use drones and install monitors to track odour-causing chemicals. Treatment can absorb, chemically change or burn away target compounds, but experts say it can be expensive; some cheaper masking sprays are viewed sceptically. Even with better evidence, people’s sensitivity to smells differs.

content.headline: Anthropic researchers warn of self-replicating AI worms, but experts differ on U
content.shortHeadline: AI worm warning draws both concern and scepticism
content.standfirst: Anthropic researchers say a test program spread across internet-connected televisions by splitting its workload. They warn future systems could adapt to more devices, while other security experts say the demonstrated worm was slow and not yet a major practical threat.

sources.originalTitle: What are self-replicating ‘AI worms’, and why is Anthropic worried about them?

segments.body: Anthropic’s offensive research team says it built a malicious AI program that spread through internet-connected televisions, dividing parts of itself among 15 devices. The researchers warn that a more capable program able to run on less powerful hardware could become feasible by the end of the year. The report describes a test, not a widespread outbreak.

segments.title: How serious is the threat?
segments.body: Some experts say AI could help malicious software adapt to new vulnerabilities, and that poorly maintained smart devices can be hard to secure. Others quoted in the report argue the demonstrated program moved slowly, that worms can be detected and blocked, and that strong passwords and two-factor authentication would stop many attacks. Experts do not agree on how high this risk should rank.

content.headline: World Bank backs small AI models for low-connectivity communities
content.shortHeadline: World Bank promotes small AI built for local needs
content.standfirst: The bank says specialised models that run on phones and work in local languages could help meet needs such as farmers’ access to soil advice. That promise depends on basic infrastructure and should be weighed against concerns about jobs and unequal access.

image.caption: Small AI models designed for phones could work in places with limited connectivity.

sources.originalTitle: World Bank says ‘small AI’ could transform developing countries

segments.body: The World Bank is urging governments and partners to develop “small AI” models designed for specific tasks, local languages and limited connectivity. Its chief knowledge officer cited Indian farmers who could use a phone-based tool to access soil analysis—support that cannot readily be provided by human specialists to every small farm.

segments.title: The infrastructure gap
segments.body: The IMF’s managing director said broad access to AI depends on electricity, digital infrastructure and safeguards. The report notes that many rural schools in sub-Saharan Africa lack electricity or consistent internet access, while the IMF also warned that AI could change or eliminate a substantial share of jobs worldwide, with young people particularly exposed.

content.headline: AI agents face blocks as websites tighten access to online services
content.shortHeadline: Websites block AI agents over security and business concerns
content.standfirst: Companies including airlines, banks and retailers are restricting automated agents, complicating tech firms’ promises that AI can handle online tasks for users. Security controls, data licensing and the value of human visits are all part of the dispute.

sources.originalTitle: Websites are closing their doors to AI agents

segments.body: AI companies are promoting agents that can book, shop and manage online tasks, but many websites restrict their access. The report says Delta blocks agents from booking tickets, while JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have confirmed they block agents from accounts over security concerns. Yelp allows access only through its paid data-licensing programme.

segments.title: A less open web?
segments.body: Some businesses say agents should act on behalf of customers; others object to automated access or the loss of human visits and advertising exposure. Anti-bot safeguards can also block legitimate agents. The result may be more checks for people using websites, even when companies’ systems were designed to catch bots rather than AI assistants.

content.headline: Anthropic says AI use is reshaping its hiring and daily work
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic reports fewer junior hires and more meetings
content.standfirst: The AI company says junior employees make up a smaller share of its technical teams than in early 2025, while meeting time has risen. Its internal report offers a snapshot of one AI-heavy workplace, not proof of how AI will change hiring across the economy.

sources.originalTitle: Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings

segments.body: Anthropic’s report says the share of junior-level employees in technical departments fell from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the share of junior technical hires dropped from 27% to 9%. The company links some change to coding tools that let non-technical staff build software, but also cites the normal expansion of other business functions.

segments.title: More output, more coordination
segments.body: Anthropic reports increases in code per person, sales per representative and contracts processed, but cautions that more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact. Meeting time per employee rose 20% over the year. Some employees said AI shifted their work toward managing its output, which the company describes as creating a new demand on human attention and judgement.
